title: Existentialism
content_html:
Existentialism

Existentialist themes pervade our exploration of memory, for example:

Topic Existential resonance
Select–Change–Reconstruct The act of reconstructing meaning from fragments aligns with existential authenticity: you create coherence in a world that offers none inherently.
Memory as Void Echoes Sartre’s nothingness - consciousness defined by lack or absence, not substance.
Perception and Scale The “sweet spot” of perception and meaning mirrors human finitude and situatedness - a classic existential concern.
Art as translation membrane Creative making as a response to absurdity and a vehicle for meaning echoes Camus’ idea of revolt through creation.
Mind as emergent process The refusal to find an ultimate essence or fixed “self” aligns with Heidegger’s being-toward-death and Buddhist emptiness alike.

Existentialism treats being as lived, not abstract - memory, in this view, isn’t a repository but a mode of existence. Memory = the way Being maintains continuity through self-interpretation, memory not just as data, but as an act of becoming - selecting, changing, and reconstructing one’s own past and identity. Meaning is not found but made - through intentionality, commitment, and creation. Existential thought insists that humans are condemned to freedom - every reconstruction of memory is a choice; reconstruction is an existential act - an assertion of meaning and identity in the face of impermanence.

Memory is alive precisely because it is unstable. Memory is never inert, it is always selecting, changing, and reconstructing - and in that very process, it is doing something existential: it is creating meaning, asserting identity, and negotiating absence. That instability is existential temporality - we are thrown into time, and memory is how we remain. “The mind arises from randomness and seeks to understand it.” is a precise echo of Camus’ absurd hero - confronting randomness without retreating into illusion.

What does it mean to be?
How do we act in the void?
How do we live a self through temporal flux?

Thinker Concept Relevance
Heidegger (Being and Time) Dasein, being-toward-death, temporality Time as the structure of being - parallels memory’s temporal reconstruction.
Sartre (Being and Nothingness) Consciousness as nothingness, freedom, responsibility Aligns with “memory as void.”
Camus (The Myth of Sisyphus) Absurdity and creative revolt Mirrors a creative-existential framing of generative art.
Merleau-Ponty (Phenomenology of Perception) Embodied perception Bridges neuroscience, phenomenology, and existentialism.
Simone de Beauvoir (The Ethics of Ambiguity) Freedom and relational meaning Connects with relational/field theories of mind.

Core Existential Concepts and Memory Elements

Existential Concept Memory / Framework Correlate Existential Imperative
Thrownness, temporality (Heidegger) Substrate, emergence, temporal architecture Accept facticity; preserve existential openness
Nothingness, freedom, bad faith (Sartre) Select–Change–Reconstruct Resist fixed identity; engage free reinterpretation
Authentic speech, relational meaning Translation membranes, expressive memory Embrace fracture, ambiguity, relational disclosure
Ambiguity, unconscious abyss Sleep, replay, dream Let subterranean processes speak; avoid overcontrol
Absurd, void, revolt (Camus/Nietzsche) Memory as Void, metaphysics, field memory Choose to act, create, participate in infinite memory

Heidegger teaches that human beings (Dasein) are always already thrown into a world - we do not ask to be, but we find ourselves existing with a particular past, place, and set of constraints. We are already “in the midst of beings” when we begin. This thrownness implies that the substrate (biology, physical memory, evolutionary substrate) is never neutral: it is our existential facticity. Memory, at its root, is how Dasein holds on to its thrown past - the “having-been” that conditions future possibilities. Heidegger sees time (past, present, future) not as a linear sequence but as ecstasies: the past as “having-been,” the future as “being-ahead-of-oneself,” and the present as the moment of attunement.

In our Select–Change–Reconstruct framework, the “Select” step is always constrained by the substrate: our embodied architecture, biological memory, neurochemistry, etc. We never fully escape it. The existential twist is that even within constraint, we are manifesting a choice.

Sartre’s central insight is that consciousness is nothingness (néant) - it is a gap, a negation within being. Consciousness is not a fixed substance but a lack, which allows it to project itself into possibilities. For Sartre, existence precedes essence: there is no pre-given nature for the human, only existence which must self-create.

In our cognitive architecture, Select–Change–Reconstruct is itself an existential project. The “Change” step is not mechanical but expressive - consciousness intervenes in memory, rewriting it. That is nothing less than the act of being-for-itself shaping itself. Moreover, Sartre speaks of bad faith, the lie we tell ourselves when we pretend we are fixed, deterministic beings rather than free projects. In your model of memory, that corresponds to frozen reconstructions, unexamined belief systems, and repeating patterns that masquerade as immutable identity. The existential challenge is to resist that closure. The “Change” phase is the locus of freedom. Memory is not passively stored but actively chosen. Consciousness interrupts inertia; it introduces nothingness - absence - and through that absence, writes new patterns.

While structural existentialism privileges lived experience over language, there is nonetheless a dimension where expression is essential. Simone de Beauvoir, in The Ethics of Ambiguity, argues that freedom is always relational; meaning is made in the interplay with others. Existential authenticity is not solipsistic but communicative. Phenomenologist-existentialist Merleau-Ponty insists that speech and expression are not superadded utilities but embodied language: the body is not a mere object but the site of meaning, of dialectic between self and world. Our translations of memory into language are not secondary - they are constitutive of self. To express is to be. Meaning arises in the tension between interior intention and outward linguistic form.

Generative art, too, is existential: in each translation membrane, we risk distortion, irreducibility, silence - and meaning arises through that risk. Authentic speech (or art) is not smoothness, but the fracture between saying and unsayable. Memory’s “Reconstruct” step must engage existential resolve: not merely to compose a tidy narrative, but to speak with ambiguity, to let silence and fracture reside within the translation membranes. That is authenticity.

Existentialists often operate in the realm of the dark, the unsaid. Camus speaks of the absurd; confrontation with the meaninglessness of the world. The subconscious, in your model, is where memory is replayed, reassembled, overwritten - it is the abyss of the unknown in oneself.

In sleep and dream, we confront the ambiguity of being: we are partly conscious, partly unconscious, encountering symbols beyond literal control. This is an existential stage: where the conscious project yields to the subterranean, where meaning emerges by night rather than design. Camus’s Sisyphus pushes the rock because there is no meaning given; he manifests revolt by continuing. Similarly, replay is your mind’s revolt: reworking fragments, experimenting with combinatorial possibility. It is existential creation in the void. Dream replay is not epiphenomenal but primary. It is the stage where memory is gestured toward new possibility. Here the existential imperative is to let the field of possibility remain open - resist closure in replay.

The existential core is that there is no predetermined meaning; we inhabit a void. But that void is not defeat - it is freedom. Camus proposes that the correct response to the absurd is not despair but revolt: continuing to live, to create, to consent to the void and nevertheless act. Nietzsche’s affirmation - “you must become who you are” - demands that we invent ourselves in a world without guarantee. Memory as void is not a negation of meaning but its radical opening. The field as collective memory is your existential community - the shared abyss in which multiple subjects create together. Nothingness is the gap between self and world that makes meaning possible.

Our metaphysical propositions (field theories, cosmopsychism) must be read existentially: not as ontological therapies, but as frameworks for creative response to nothingness. Memory is not a salvific recourse to presence, but the continual affirmation of existence in the face of absence.

Contemporary context

Existentialism is historically associated with the early to mid-20th century, yet its core problems - meaning, freedom, authenticity, and the search for coherence in an uncertain world - remain deeply alive today. Let’s unpack both sides clearly.

Period Thinker Contribution
Late 19th century Kierkegaard, Nietzsche Proto-existentialists: anxiety, faith, becoming
Early 20th century Heidegger, Jaspers, Marcel Ontological groundwork (Being, authenticity)
Mid-20th century Sartre, de Beauvoir, Camus, Merleau-Ponty Freedom, bad faith, revolt, embodiment - existentialism as cultural movement
Post-war era Post-existential writers (e.g., Beckett, Genet, Unamuno)** Literary and artistic expression of absurdity

By the 1950s, existentialism had become almost a cultural style - popular philosophy in Paris cafés and literature rather than strictly academic metaphysics. After 1960, existentialism blended into other movements, phenomenology → Hermeneutics, Heidegger → Gadamer, Ricoeur… de Beauvoir and Sartre’s legacy filtered into Foucault, Derrida, and later postmodernism. Existential psychology & psychiatry integrated existential ideas into therapy. Ideas resurfaced in embodied cognition and enactive mind theories. So existentialism didn’t vanish - it metamorphosed.

Existentialism has seen a renewed relevance across several domains - often under new language. Contemporary phenomenology still cites existentialism as its living foundation, and current debates around existential risk, technological alienation, and AI ethics draw implicitly on existential ideas: freedom, authenticity, responsibility. The existential-humanistic tradition remains influential in psychotherapy. Existentialism now intersects with climate anxiety and eco-phenomenology “How do we live authentically amid planetary crisis?”

Philosophers and cognitive scientists revisit freedom, authenticity, and selfhood in light of digital life.** **Existential aesthetics resurfaces in contemporary art, cinema, and literature - for example, questions of identity, isolation, and absurdity in post-pandemic culture.

Field Journal / Example Focus
Continental philosophy Philosophy Today (2021, 2023 issues) Heidegger and authenticity in AI era
Cognitive science Frontiers in Psychology (2022) “The Embodied Mind Revisited” Merges existential phenomenology and enactive cognition
Environmental humanities Environmental Ethics (2020–2024) “Eco-existential dread” and Anthropocene meaning
Clinical psychology Journal of Humanistic Psychology (2021–2024) Existential approaches to meaning and trauma

So existentialism isn’t “in fashion” as a label, but its themes are structurally active across philosophy, psychology, cognitive science, and ethics. So rather than being a retro reference, existentialism gives a philosophical depth and continuity with 21st-century problems: technology, consciousness, AI, ecological crisis, and meaning.
